about.p: About 220 words at C1–C2 level that you meet in novels, newspapers and good conversation, but that are not in the other courses here: words like *patronise*, *sycophantic*, *livid* and *dither*. They describe people, attitudes and behaviour, so they are the words that make your English sound precise.

about.kr: 이 책은 다른 과정에 없는 C1~C2 단어만 모았어요. *patronise*(아랫사람 대하듯 하다)처럼 사람의 태도와 행동을 정확하게 그려 주는 단어들이에요. 단어마다 한국어 뜻과 함께 한국어 접점, 뿌리와 가족, 덩어리 표현, 헷갈리는 이웃 단어를 붙였어요. 비슷한 단어끼리 한 단원에 모아서 차이를 비교하며 배우게 했어요.

about.tip: These words carry feeling. *Frugal* praises, *stingy* criticises; *confident* is good, *smug* is not. Always learn whether a word approves or disapproves.

L.kr: 한국어에는 '무시하다', '깔보다', '아랫사람 대하듯 하다'가 있어요. 영어는 이것을 더 잘게 나눠요. 겉으로는 친절하게 굴면서 낮춰 보는 것은 *patronise*, 말투로 내려다보는 것은 *condescending*, 상대의 성과를 작게 만드는 것은 *belittle*이에요. 영국 영어는 *patronise*, 미국 영어는 *patronize*로 써요.

L.p: When Mia started at the firm, an older colleague explained the photocopier to her slowly, as if she were a child. He was *patronising* her: being kind on the surface while treating her as less intelligent. His *condescending* tone, the voice of someone who feels superior, made it worse. When she won a big client, he *belittled* the success, saying that anyone could have done it, and he liked to *disparage* the younger staff in meetings, criticising them in a way that showed no respect. Mia's ideas were usually met with a *dismissive* wave of the hand, as if they were not worth thinking about.

His friend in the finance department was worse. She had a *supercilious* smile, the smile of someone who thinks she is better than everyone else. After a good year she was *smug*, far too pleased with herself. She would *sneer* at people's clothes, smiling with one side of her mouth, and make *snide* remarks that sounded harmless but were meant to hurt. Her decisions were *high-handed*: she never asked anyone's opinion.

L.x: You *patronise* someone (not *patronise to someone*). In British English, *patronise* also means to be a customer of a shop: *the shops that we patronise*.

L.tip: *Smug* is about being pleased with yourself. *Supercilious* is about looking down on others. A person can be both.

patronise.l: 한국어 '무시하다'보다 교묘해요. 겉으로는 친절하고 차근차근 설명하지만 '너는 모르지?' 하는 태도가 깔려 있어요. 한국어로는 '애 취급하다'가 가장 가까워요.
patronise.r: *patron*(후원자)에서 왔어요. 후원자가 도움받는 사람을 내려다보는 태도라는 뜻이에요. 형용사는 *patronising*(가르치려 드는).
patronise.n: *condescend*도 거의 같지만 말투와 태도에 초점이 있어요. *patronise*는 '친절을 가장한' 무시라는 점이 핵심이에요.

condescending.l: 한국어 '거들먹거리다', '하대하다'와 같은 느낌이에요. 영어도 '자리에서 내려온다'는 그림이에요.
condescending.r: 라틴어 *con-* + *descendere*(내려오다). 높은 사람이 일부러 몸을 낮춘다는 뜻에서 '잘난 척하며 낮춰 본다'로 변했어요.
condescending.n: *patronising*은 친절을 가장한 무시이고, *condescending*은 대놓고 우월함을 드러내는 태도예요.

belittle.n: *underestimate*는 실력을 낮게 보는 실수이고, *belittle*은 일부러 작게 만드는 거예요.

disparage.l: 한국어 '폄하하다'예요. 격식 있는 글에 쓰는 말이에요.
disparage.r: 고대 프랑스어 *desparagier*(신분이 낮은 사람과 결혼시키다). '격을 떨어뜨리다'에서 왔어요. 형용사는 *disparaging*.
disparage.n: *criticise*는 좋은 비판도 포함하지만, *disparage*는 존중 없이 깎아내리는 거예요.

dismissive.l: 한국어 '콧방귀 뀌다', '귓등으로 듣다'와 같은 태도예요. 뒤에 *of*를 써요.
c: a dismissive wave of the hand
dismissive.n: *rude*는 무례한 것이고, *dismissive*는 상대의 말을 들을 가치도 없다는 듯 넘기는 거예요.

supercilious.l: 한국어 '콧대 높은', '눈을 내리깔고 보는'이에요. 영어는 '눈썹을 올린다'는 그림이에요.
supercilious.r: 라틴어 *supercilium*(눈썹). 거만한 사람이 눈썹을 치켜올리는 모습에서 왔어요.
supercilious.n: *arrogant*는 자기를 과대평가하는 것이고, *supercilious*는 그 마음이 얼굴과 태도로 드러나 남을 깔보는 거예요.

smug.l: 한국어 '의기양양'은 좋은 뜻도 있지만 *smug*은 늘 얄밉다는 뜻이에요. '잘난 척 히죽거리는' 느낌이에요.
smug.n: *proud*는 좋은 뜻일 수 있고, *smug*은 남이 보기에 얄미운 자기만족이에요. 3과의 *complacent*는 그래서 방심하는 거고요.

sneer.l: 한국어 '비웃다', '코웃음 치다'와 같아요. 입꼬리 한쪽을 올리는 모습이에요.
sneer.r: 원래 말이 콧김을 내뿜는 소리를 가리켰을 거라고 해요. 명사로도 써요: *a sneer*.
sneer.n: *laugh at*은 소리 내어 웃는 것이고, *sneer*는 얼굴이나 말로 경멸을 드러내는 거예요.

snide.l: 한국어 '뼈 있는 말', '돌려 까기'가 이 단어예요. 겉으로는 별말 아닌데 상처를 주려는 말이에요.
snide.n: *sarcastic*은 반대로 말해서 비꼬는 것이고, *snide*는 은근히, 몰래 깎아내리는 거예요.

high-handed.n: *bossy*는 일상어로 '이래라저래라 하는', *high-handed*는 권한을 내세워 남의 의견을 무시하는 거예요.

units.O: Describe someone who patronised you, or a time when you were treated in a condescending way. What did they say or do, and how did you react?

L.kr: 한국어에는 '아부하다', '아첨하다', '비위를 맞추다', '굽신거리다', '알랑거리다'가 있어요. 영어도 아주 많아요. 그런데 영어 단어 대부분이 '몸'으로 그림을 그려요. 바닥을 기고(*grovel*), 꼬리를 흔들고(*fawn*), 기름을 바르듯 미끄럽고(*unctuous*), 버터를 발라 줘요(*butter up*). 한국어 '아부'와 '비위'는 몸이 아니라 마음에서 오는 말이에요.

L.p: Every office has one. Gary is *sycophantic*: he praises the boss far too much in order to get something from her. He tries to *ingratiate himself* with anyone powerful, laughing at their jokes and remembering their birthdays. He *curries favour* with the directors by offering to work at weekends. When the chairman visits, Gary *fawns* over him like a puppy, and when he makes a mistake he *grovels*, apologising as if he were on his knees.

His colleagues have less polite words for him. To them he is a *toady*, someone who does whatever powerful people want. Some say he *brown-noses* the boss, a rude expression. His manner is *unctuous*, smooth and too polite in a way that is not sincere, and his attitude to the directors is *servile*, as if he were their servant. Before asking for a pay rise he always *butters up* his manager with compliments.

L.x: You *ingratiate yourself with* someone (not *ingratiate someone*). You *curry favour with* someone (not *curry favour to* someone).

L.tip: *Brown-nose* is rude. Use it only with friends. In writing, choose *sycophantic* or *ingratiate yourself*.

sycophantic.r: 그리스어 *sykophantes*(밀고자). 원래 남을 고발해 이득을 보는 사람이었는데, 영어에서 '아첨꾼'이 됐어요.
sycophantic.n: *flattering*은 칭찬하는 말 자체이고, *sycophantic*은 이득을 노린 지나친 아부라는 비판이에요.

ingratiate yourself.r: 라틴어 *in gratiam*(호의 안으로). *grace*, *gratitude*와 뿌리가 같아요. 형용사는 *ingratiating*.
ingratiate yourself.n: *curry favour*는 이득을 얻으려 아부하는 행동이고, *ingratiate yourself*는 좋아하게 만들려는 시도 전체예요.

curry favour.r: 옛 프랑스어 *Fauvel*(중세 풍자 이야기에 나오는 교활한 말)을 빗질한다(*curry*)는 말에서 왔어요.
curry favour.n: *butter up*은 칭찬으로 기분을 맞추는 일상어이고, *curry favour*는 더 격식 있고 비판적이에요.

fawn.l: 한국어 '알랑거리다', '꼬리를 치다'와 같아요. 영어도 개가 꼬리를 흔드는 그림이에요.
fawn.r: 고대 영어 *fagnian*(기뻐하다). 개가 반가워 꼬리 치는 모습에서 왔어요. 아기 사슴 *fawn*과 철자가 같지만 다른 말이에요.
fawn.n: *admire*는 진심으로 존경하는 것이고, *fawn over*는 그것을 지나치게 드러내 비굴해 보이는 거예요.

grovel.l: 한국어 '굽신거리다', '무릎 꿇고 빌다'와 같은 그림이에요. 영어는 '바닥에 엎드려 기다'예요.
grovel.n: *apologise*는 그냥 사과하는 것이고, *grovel*은 자존심을 다 버리고 비는 거예요.

a toady.r: *toad-eater*(두꺼비를 먹는 사람)의 줄임말이에요. 옛날 떠돌이 약장수의 조수가 독이 있다는 두꺼비를 먹는 척하는 일을 했어요. 주인을 위해 무엇이든 하는 사람이라는 뜻이에요.
a toady.n: *a yes-man*은 무조건 찬성하는 사람이고, *a toady*는 아첨으로 이득을 노리는 사람이에요.

brown-nose.l: 한국어로도 비속한 말이에요. 친구끼리 놀릴 때만 쓰고 글에서는 쓰지 마세요.
brown-nose.r: 무례한 그림에서 온 미국 군대 속어예요. 영국에서는 *suck up to*도 많이 써요.
brown-nose.n: 뜻은 *curry favour*와 같지만 아주 무례한 말이에요.

unctuous.l: 한국어 '느끼하다', '능글맞다'에 가까워요. 영어는 '기름 바른 듯 미끈한' 그림이에요.
unctuous.n: *polite*는 좋은 뜻이고, *unctuous*는 지나치게 매끄러워 믿음이 안 가는 정중함이에요.

servile.n: *obedient*는 말을 잘 듣는 좋은 뜻일 수 있지만, *servile*은 자존심 없이 비굴하다는 뜻이에요.

butter up.l: 한국어 '입에 발린 소리를 하다', '꼬드기다'예요. 영어는 '빵에 버터를 바르듯' 그림이에요.

units.O: Describe someone who flatters people in power: at work, at school or in politics. What do they do, and how do others react? Use four words from this unit.

L.kr: 화를 말하는 영어 단어는 '얼마나 화났나'와 '어떻게 화났나'로 갈려요. *irate*와 *livid*는 몹시 화난 것, *seethe*는 속으로 부글부글 끓는 것, *petulant*와 *sulk*는 아이처럼 토라지는 것이에요. 한국어 '열받다'는 *seethe*, '삐지다'는 *sulk*, '울화통이 터지다'는 *exasperated*에 가까워요.

L.p: The flight was delayed for the third time, and the passengers were *exasperated*: they had run out of patience completely. One *irate* businessman, very angry indeed, demanded to see a manager. A woman whose wedding was the next day was *livid*, pale with fury. Others sat quietly and *seethed*, angry inside without showing it. Many were *indignant*, angry because they had been treated unfairly, and it was *galling*, painfully annoying, to watch the airline staff leave for the night.

Some anger is childish. A *petulant* child who cannot have what he wants stamps his feet, and a teenager who is told off may *sulk* in his room for hours, refusing to speak. Some people are *irascible*: they lose their temper easily. And some anger lasts. A small insult from years ago can still *rankle*, staying in your mind and continuing to annoy you.

L.x: People *seethe with* anger (not *seethe by* anger). You are *indignant at* or *about* something (not *indignant of* it).

L.tip: *Livid* first meant bluish-grey, the colour of a bruise. A face turns that colour in great anger.

exasperated.l: 한국어 '속 터진다', '울화통이 터지다'예요. 같은 일이 계속되어 참을성이 바닥난 거예요.
exasperated.n: *annoyed*는 가볍게 짜증 난 것이고, *exasperated*는 오래 참다가 한계에 이른 거예요.

irate.l: 한국어 '격분한'이에요. 신문 기사에서 고객, 시민, 승객에 자주 붙어요.
irate.n: *angry*의 강한 말이에요. *livid*는 그보다 더 세서 얼굴빛이 변할 정도예요.

livid.l: 한국어 '얼굴이 붉으락푸르락하다'와 같은 그림이에요. 영국 구어에서 아주 많이 써요.
livid.r: 라틴어 *lividus*(푸르스름한). 원래 멍 든 살갗의 색이었어요.
livid.n: *irate*는 기사에서 쓰는 말이고, *livid*는 대화에서 쓰는 더 센 말이에요.

seethe.n: *rage*는 겉으로 터지는 분노이고, *seethe*는 안에서 끓는 분노예요.

L.kr: 속임수를 말하는 영어 단어는 '속이는 사람'과 '속는 사람'으로 나눠 외우면 쉬워요. 속이는 쪽은 *deceitful*, *devious*, *guile*, 속이는 방법은 *a ploy*, *a ruse*, *a swindle*, 속는 쪽은 *dupe*예요. *hoodwink*는 한국어 '눈 가리고 아웅'처럼 '눈을 가린다'는 그림이에요.

L.p: The fraud trial lasted six weeks. The accused man was *deceitful*: he lied easily and often. He was also *devious*, using clever, hidden methods to get what he wanted. With charm and *guile*, a clever kind of dishonesty, he had *beguiled* hundreds of pensioners, charming them into trusting him. They were completely *hoodwinked*, tricked into believing that their money was safe.

The scheme was *fraudulent* from the start, designed to cheat. The free lunch for investors was a *ploy*, a clever plan to get them to sign. Another *ruse* was a fake letter from a bank. In the end he *swindled* them out of four million pounds. Many victims said that they felt like *dupes*, people who had been easily fooled.

L.x: You *swindle someone out of* money (not *swindle money from someone* in the same pattern). People are *hoodwinked into* doing something (not *hoodwinked to* do it).

L.tip: *Beguile* can also be positive: a *beguiling* smile is charming and attractive. Only the context tells you whether there is a trick.

beguile.n: *charm*은 좋은 뜻이고, *beguile*은 매혹이 속임으로 이어질 수 있다는 느낌이 있어요.

L.kr: 칭찬과 꾸중도 세기가 다른 단어가 많아요. 꾸중은 약한 순서로 *chide*(가볍게 나무라다), *rebuke*와 *reprimand*(꾸짖다), *berate*(호되게 야단치다), *lambast*(맹비난하다), *vilify*(악인으로 몰다)예요. *reprimand*는 회사나 군대의 공식 징계에 써요. 칭찬은 *commend*와 *laud*, 본보기가 될 만큼 훌륭하면 *exemplary*예요.

L.p: The judge *commended* the firefighters, praising them officially for their bravery. Newspapers *lauded* the youngest of them, a twenty-year-old who had carried two children out of the building, and her conduct was described as *exemplary*, so good that others should copy it.

The fire chief was treated very differently. The minister *chided* him gently for a slow response, and then *rebuked* him more sharply in a letter. He was formally *reprimanded* by the fire service. At a public meeting an angry resident *berated* him for twenty minutes, shouting and criticising him. The press *lambasted* the service as a whole, and one paper *vilified* the chief, writing as if he were an evil man. An official report later *censured* the council as well, criticising it formally for cutting the budget.

L.x: You *rebuke someone for* doing something (not *rebuke someone to* do it). *Commend someone for* their courage (not *commend someone their* courage).

L.tip: The blame words go from soft to hard: *chide*, *rebuke*, *reprimand*, *berate*, *lambast*, *vilify*.

L.kr: 용기 단어는 칭찬하는 말과 꼬집는 말이 섞여 있어요. *intrepid*, *plucky*, *undaunted*는 칭찬이고, *audacious*는 칭찬일 때도 '뻔뻔하다'일 때도 있어요. 두려움 쪽은 '조마조마'(*trepidation*), '걱정스러운'(*apprehensive*), '양심에 걸림'(*qualms*)처럼 이유가 달라요. *qualms*는 무섭다기보다 '마음에 걸린다'는 뜻이에요.

L.p: The *intrepid* explorer, fearless and adventurous, set off across the ice alone. Storms did not stop her: she was *undaunted*, still determined in spite of the danger. Her plan to reach the pole in winter was *audacious*, bold enough to shock people. Newspapers called her *plucky*, a friendly word for someone small who shows courage, and her friends said she had real *mettle*, the strength of character to face hard things.

Her family felt only *trepidation*, nervous fear about what might happen. Her mother was *apprehensive* every time the phone rang. The size of the task was *daunting*: it made even experienced sailors lose confidence. The *faint-hearted*, people without courage, should never try it. And her sponsor had *qualms* about the whole adventure: he felt uneasy, wondering whether it was right to pay for something so dangerous.

L.x: You have *qualms about* something (not *qualms for* it). A task is *daunting* (not *daunted*); a person is *undaunted*.

L.tip: *Audacious* praises boldness but can also mean shameless: *an audacious lie* is a lie told with no shame at all.

mettle.n: *courage*는 용기 자체이고, *mettle*은 어려움을 견디는 성품의 단단함이에요.

apprehensive.n: *afraid*보다 약하고, 다가올 일이 잘못될까 걱정하는 거예요.

L.kr: 말하는 방식을 나타내는 단어는 '말이 많다'와 '말이 적다' 두 줄로 정리하면 쉬워요. 많은 쪽은 *verbose*, *long-winded*, *loquacious*, *waffle*, 적은 쪽은 *laconic*, *terse*, *curt*, *reticent*예요. 하나 더, *glib*는 말은 술술 나오는데 진심이 없는 거예요. 한국어 '입만 살았다'가 *glib*예요.

L.p: Some speakers never stop. A *verbose* report uses far more words than it needs. A *long-winded* speech goes on and on until the audience falls asleep. A *loquacious* taxi driver talks happily for the whole journey, and a student who does not know the answer may *waffle*, talking for a long time without saying anything useful.

L.h: B Too few, or the wrong kind

L.p: Others say very little. A *laconic* farmer answers in three words, and his humour is dry. A *terse* email from the boss, short and slightly unfriendly, can ruin your morning, and a *curt* reply is rude in its shortness. A *reticent* person does not like to talk about private feelings. Someone *inarticulate* cannot express ideas clearly, however clever they are. And a *glib* politician gives smooth, easy answers that sound good but show no real thought.

L.x: People *waffle on about* something (not *waffle at* it). A *reticent* person is reserved; do not confuse it with *reluctant* (unwilling).

L.tip: *Laconic* is often a compliment: short and wise. *Curt* and *terse* are criticisms: short and unfriendly.

L.kr: 성격 단어도 칭찬과 비판이 짝을 이뤄요. 꼼꼼함이 지나치면 *meticulous*(칭찬)에서 *fastidious*(까다로운), *pedantic*(쩨쩨하게 따지는)로 넘어가요. 가벼움은 *frivolous*(경박한)와 *flippant*(진지한 일에 가볍게 구는)이고, 그 반대가 *earnest*(진지한)예요. *stoic*은 고대 그리스 철학자들에게서 온 말로, '불평 없이 참는' 성품이에요.

L.p: Our new editor is *meticulous*: she checks every comma with great care. She is also *fastidious*, very fussy about cleanliness and detail; she will not use anyone else's pen. Sometimes she becomes *pedantic*, correcting tiny mistakes that nobody else cares about. Her assistant is quite different. He is *quirky*, with strange but charming habits, such as eating his lunch standing on one leg.

The sales team are *frivolous*: they treat serious things as if they were games. When the boss announced job cuts, one of them made a *flippant* joke, showing no respect for the seriousness of the news. By contrast, the new graduate is *earnest*, very serious and sincere. The finance director is *stoic*: when her department was closed she did not complain once. And the founder was famously *impetuous*, acting quickly without thinking, and *headstrong*, determined to do what he wanted whatever anyone said.

L.x: A person is *fastidious about* cleanliness (not *fastidious of* it). Do not confuse *earnest* (sincere) with *honest* (truthful).

L.tip: *Meticulous* is praise. *Pedantic* is the same carefulness, but annoying.

units.O: Describe three people you know, using words from this unit. Is each word praise or criticism?

L.kr: 돈 쓰는 단어는 '많이 쓴다'와 '아낀다'가 각각 칭찬과 비판으로 갈려요. 많이 쓰는 쪽에서 *lavish*는 '아낌없는'(칭찬도 가능), *extravagant*와 *profligate*는 '낭비하는'(비판)이에요. 아끼는 쪽에서는 *frugal*(검소한, 이미 배움)이 칭찬이고 *tight-fisted*와 *penny-pinching*은 '짠돌이'라는 비판이에요. 부유함은 *affluent*, *well-heeled*, *opulent*로 말해요.

L.p: For their wedding the couple threw a *lavish* party, generous and expensive, with three hundred guests. Buying a sports car on a teacher's salary was *extravagant*, costing more than they could reasonably afford. After their first pay rise they decided to *splurge* on a holiday, spending a lot on one special thing. Her uncle was less sensible: he was *profligate*, wasting money until he had none left. The hotel they stayed in was *opulent*, rich and luxurious, with gold taps.

The couple come from different backgrounds. She grew up in an *affluent* suburb, where most families had plenty of money, among *well-heeled* neighbours with expensive cars. His family were often *hard up*, short of money at the end of each month. His father was *tight-fisted*, unwilling to spend anything, and his mother's *penny-pinching*, her habit of saving every possible penny, kept the family going.

L.x: You *splurge on* something (not *splurge for* it). A person is *hard up* (not *hard down*).

L.tip: *Lavish* can be praise (*lavish praise*, generous) or criticism (*lavish spending*). *Extravagant* and *profligate* are always criticism.

L.kr: 일이 힘든 이유는 여러 가지예요. 몸이 힘들면 *strenuous*, *back-breaking*, 시간과 공이 많이 들면 *painstaking*, *laborious*, 부담과 책임이 무거우면 *onerous*, 지루하게 반복되면 *drudgery*, 기준이 높아서 힘들면 *exacting*이에요. 한국어 '노가다'는 *slog*, *toil*에 가까워요. 반대로 힘들지 않으면 *effortless*예요.

L.p: Building the stone wall by hand was *back-breaking* work, so physically hard that it hurt. Each stone had to be fitted with *painstaking* care, every detail checked. The paperwork was *laborious*, needing a lot of slow, careful effort, and the safety rules placed *onerous* duties on the owner, heavy and difficult to fulfil. The architect was *exacting*, demanding the highest standards.

The workers *toiled* from dawn to dusk, working long and hard. One of them called the job a *slog*, a long period of hard, boring work. For the young apprentice, sweeping up every evening was pure *drudgery*: dull, tiring work with no interest at all. A climb up the hill each morning was *strenuous*, needing great physical effort. Yet the old stonemason made it all look *effortless*, as if it needed no effort.

L.p: The talks about the new airport were *contentious* from the start: people argued fiercely about them. The local council was *adamant* that there would be no new runway; it said so firmly and would not change its mind. The airline was equally *intransigent*, refusing every compromise, and its chairman was *unyielding*. Residents were *defiant*, openly refusing to obey the planning order, and a few *recalcitrant* landowners would not cooperate at all. One elderly farmer was *obdurate*: nothing anyone said could move him.

In the end, a new minister found people who were more *amenable*, willing to listen and to agree. Some residents were *compliant*, ready to do what they were told, which made the work easier. Critics said that the council had become too *pliable*, easily influenced by the airline. Others said the new deal was simply realistic.

L.kr: 착함과 잔인함도 이유와 방식으로 갈려요. 너그럽게 용서하면 *magnanimous*, 돈을 기부하면 *philanthropic*, 남이 잘되길 바라면 *benevolent*이에요. 잔인한 쪽은 아무 감정이 없으면 *callous*, *heartless*, 목적을 위해 수단을 안 가리면 *ruthless*, 복수하려 하면 *vindictive*, 쩨쩨하게 괴롭히면 *spiteful*, 해치려는 마음이 있으면 *malevolent*예요. *benign*은 '순한, 양성(종양)'이에요.

L.p: The old factory owner was *benevolent*: he wanted good things for everyone who worked for him. After making his fortune he became *philanthropic*, giving millions to hospitals and schools. When he won a long court case against a rival, he was *magnanimous*, forgiving him and offering him a job. People who met him described his smile as *benign*, gentle and kind.

His son was very different. He was *ruthless* in business, willing to hurt anyone to get what he wanted. He was *callous* about the workers he sacked, showing no sympathy at all, and some called him *heartless*. When a manager complained, the son was *vindictive*: he tried for years to damage the man's career. His sister was merely *spiteful*, saying small cruel things to annoy people. But the family's lawyer had a *malevolent* look, as if he wished everyone harm.

L.tip: *Ruthless* can be admired in sport or business: *a ruthless striker*. *Callous* and *vindictive* never are.

L.kr: '해롭다'를 영어는 해로움의 방식으로 나눠요. 죽일 수 있으면 *lethal*, 냄새나 연기처럼 독하면 *noxious*, 서서히 몰래 퍼지면 *insidious*와 *pernicious*, 어떤 것에 손해가 되면 *detrimental*과 *deleterious*, 힘을 빼면 *debilitating*이에요. 반대로 해가 없으면 *innocuous*, 몸과 마음에 좋으면 *wholesome*, 괴롭지만 교훈이 되면 *salutary*예요. 한국어 '쓴 약'처럼 아픈데 이로운 것이 *salutary*예요.

L.p: The factory leaked a *noxious* gas, poisonous and unpleasant to breathe. In large amounts it could be *lethal*, able to kill. Its effects on children's lungs were *detrimental*, causing harm, and doctors warned of *deleterious* effects on the heart, a formal word for harmful. The illness it caused was *debilitating*, making people weak for months. Worst of all, the damage was *insidious*: it spread slowly and secretly, so nobody noticed until it was too late. Campaigners called the company's influence on the town *pernicious*, harmful in a gradual, hidden way.

The company said that the gas was *innocuous*, completely harmless. Nobody believed it. The town now promotes *wholesome* things instead: fresh food, clean air and outdoor sport. The disaster was a *salutary* lesson, unpleasant but useful, which taught the council to inspect every factory.

L.x: Something is *detrimental to* health (not *detrimental for* health). A *salutary* lesson is useful; do not confuse it with *salary*.

L.tip: *Insidious* and *pernicious* both describe slow, hidden harm. *Insidious* stresses that you do not notice it; *pernicious* stresses how much damage it does.

L.kr: 양을 말하는 단어는 형태가 다양해요. '넘침'은 *a plethora*, *a glut*, *copious*, *plentiful*, *myriad*이고 '모자람'은 *a dearth*, *scarce*, *scant*, *meagre*, *paltry*예요. 조심할 것이 둘 있어요. *a glut*은 '너무 많아서 문제'이고, *paltry*는 '쥐꼬리만 한'이라고 비웃는 말이에요. 또 *scarce*와 *scant*는 쓰는 자리가 달라요.

L.p: In the summer there is *a glut* of strawberries: so many that farmers cannot sell them all. Supermarkets offer *a plethora* of brands, far more than anyone needs. Rain is *plentiful* in the west, and the hills are home to *myriad* insects, so many that they cannot be counted. The cook used *copious* amounts of cream, a very large quantity.

In winter the picture changes. Fresh fruit becomes *scarce*, hard to find because there is not enough. There is *a dearth* of jobs in the villages, and the few that exist pay *meagre* wages, too small to live on comfortably. Workers were offered a *paltry* pay rise of one per cent, so small that it was almost an insult. The council paid *scant* attention to their complaints, very little attention.

L.x: *Scant* goes before a noun (*scant attention*); *scarce* usually comes after the verb (*Water is scarce*). The spelling is *meagre* in British English and *meager* in American English.

L.tip: *Myriad* can be used like an adjective (*myriad insects*) or a noun (*a myriad of insects*). Both are correct.

L.kr: 시간 단어는 '짧은가, 긴가'와 '곧 오는가'로 나눠요. 짧게 사라지면 *ephemeral*, *short-lived*, 오래가면 *enduring*, *abiding*, *perennial*, *perpetual*이에요. 곧 닥치면 *imminent*, *impending*이고, 잠시 쓰는 것은 *interim*, *provisional*이에요. 한국어 '임시'에 해당하는 말이 둘인데, *interim*은 '다음 것이 올 때까지', *provisional*은 '아직 확정 전'이에요.

L.p: Fame on the internet is *ephemeral*: it lasts a day, then disappears. The singer's first success was *short-lived*, lasting only a few months. Yet her love of music was *enduring*, lasting all her life, and her *abiding* memory of childhood was her grandmother singing in the kitchen. Some problems are *perennial*, returning again and again, like the shortage of nurses every winter. And the city was in a state of *perpetual* noise, never stopping for a moment.

L.h: B Coming soon and for now

L.p: When the old manager resigned, the board appointed an *interim* director, who would lead the company until a permanent one was found. Her first budget was *provisional*, likely to change once the final figures arrived. Staff could sense *impending* change, something that was about to happen. Then came the news that a takeover was *imminent*, likely to happen at any moment.

L.x: Danger is *imminent* (not *eminent*, which means famous and respected). A plan is *provisional* (not *provisory*).

L.tip: *Imminent* and *impending* are almost the same, but *imminent* is closer in time: it could happen today.

L.kr: 분명한 정도를 나타내는 단어예요. 분명한 쪽은 *lucid*(명쾌한), *unequivocal*(두말할 여지 없는), *self-explanatory*(설명이 필요 없는)이고, 불분명한 쪽은 *cryptic*(수수께끼 같은), *nebulous*(뜬구름 같은), *obscure*(잘 알려지지 않은, 모호한), *abstruse*(난해한), *muddled*(뒤죽박죽인)예요. 한국 문화와 특히 잘 맞는 단어가 *tacit*이에요. 말하지 않아도 서로 아는 '암묵적인' 동의예요.

L.p: The professor's lecture was *abstruse*, so difficult that only experts could follow it. His notes were *cryptic*, with a hidden meaning that nobody could work out. He referred to an *obscure* poet, one that hardly anyone had heard of. His plans for the department were *nebulous*, vague and without any clear shape, and his arguments were *muddled*, confused and badly organised. The students found the whole course *intricate*, with so many small parts that it was hard to see the whole.

The new lecturer was the opposite. Her explanations were *lucid*, clear and easy to understand. Her answer to the question of cheating was *unequivocal*: anyone caught would fail. The instructions on her handouts were *self-explanatory*, so nobody needed to ask questions. And there was a *tacit* agreement among the students, understood without anyone saying it, that nobody would be late to her class.

L.x: An agreement that nobody states is *tacit* (not *tactic*, which is a plan). A *self-explanatory* form needs no explanation (not *self-explaining*).

L.tip: *Cryptic* is not always bad: a *cryptic crossword* is a puzzle that British newspapers print every day, full of clever hidden meanings.
